accounts.prose: This is the package-facing barrel: it implements no merge logic, but exposes `merge`, `mergeAndCompare`, `mergeAndConcat`, `concatArrays`, and the `Merge` type from two delegated modules. The README presents the package as recursive plain-object merging with special instances retained as values. One documented edge is overstated: `merge(x)` is said to always return a new object, but the implementation’s empty reduction returns `x` itself.

referent.description: public merge-anything entry module

qualifications: Static TypeScript/source interpretation only; runtime, emitted-package, and loader behavior were not executed.
README statements are attributed documentation, not established behavior. The no-additional-arguments discrepancy follows directly from the implementation and README text.
The entry module uses wildcard re-exports, so its apparent API follows the compiler-observed exports of the delegated modules.

accounts.prose: The public `Merge<T, Ts>` models record inputs by repeatedly deep-merging tuple members in order and then recursively prettifying the resulting intersection-like shape. If either side is not modeled as records, it falls back to the last newcomer type; an empty newcomer list therefore falls through `Pop` to `never` for a non-record first input, although runtime `merge(x)` returns `x`. Optional/required keys receive dedicated union and override handling.

referent.description: compile-time result-shape machinery behind the public Merge type

qualifications: These modules are type-only and do not perform runtime merging.
The type model is an approximation encoded through conditional and mapped types; no compiler test suite was inspected.
`PrettyPrint` guards against revisiting already-seen types while recursively materializing record fields.

accounts.prose: `concatArrays` is a narrow conflict policy: when both old and new values are arrays it returns their concatenation; otherwise it returns the new value unchanged. `mergeAndConcat` feeds this policy into the same recursive engine, so nested array conflicts concatenate while other conflicts retain normal replacement behavior.

referent.description: array-concatenation merge policy

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.
Concatenation is shallow and uses the origin array's `concat`; no element-level recursive merge is evident.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: The engine is best understood as a left fold over the additional arguments. The first argument is the initial accumulator; each newcomer is merged into that accumulator, and the result becomes the input to the next step. A plain-object newcomer produces an ordinary new object for that step, while any non-plain newcomer—such as an array, primitive, function, date, or class instance—is returned as the accumulator unchanged by the engine. Consequently, “non-plain values replace” applies even at the root, and a later plain object can in turn replace or merge over that value. With no additional arguments, `merge` returns the original first argument rather than making a copy.

accounts.prose: `mergeAndConcat` is a preset use of the same callback mechanism. Its `concatArrays` callback concatenates only when both the prior and incoming values are arrays; otherwise it returns the incoming value. Thus arrays still are not recursively traversed: at an array-valued property the callback receives the two complete arrays and returns `origin.concat(incoming)`. Concatenation is shallow, so array elements retain their references. The same callback also runs at non-array properties and simply preserves normal newcomer-wins behavior there.

accounts.prose: `mergeAndCompare` performs the same fold and traversal, but computes each incoming property's final assigned value by calling `compareFn(priorValue, incomingOrRecursivelyMergedValue, key)`. The callback is invoked for every visited incoming own property except skipped `__proto__`, including a newly introduced property whose prior value is `undefined`. For an overlapping plain-object property, nested callbacks run during recursion first; the parent callback then receives the prior parent object and the already-merged child object, so it may keep, replace, or transform that entire merged child. The key may be a string or symbol.

qualifications: This is broader than the README's statement that the callback is triggered every time a value is “overwritten”; implementation also calls it for incoming properties that had no defined prior value.

accounts.prose: Recursion is driven primarily by the incoming value: it occurs when the prior value is not `undefined` and the incoming value is a plain object. If both values are plain objects, their properties combine deeply. If the prior value is defined but non-plain, recursion starts from an empty object and reconstructs the incoming plain object. If the prior value is missing or explicitly `undefined`, recursion is skipped and the incoming value is assigned directly. This explains the reference behavior precisely: origin-only properties are copied by reference; an incoming plain object with no defined counterpart is also retained by reference; only an overlapping, defined path whose incoming side is plain is rebuilt. Arrays and special objects are assigned as values rather than traversed.

referent.description: recursive-merge trigger and nested reference retention

qualifications: The implementation does not distinguish a missing prior key from an own prior key whose value is `undefined` when deciding whether to recurse.
The README similarly warns that nested references can remain linked, but its prose is user-facing guidance; the more exact branch behavior here comes from source inspection.
No cycle detection is visible in the recursive implementation, so this evidence does not support safe handling of overlapping cyclic plain-object graphs.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

@investigram-a61e09f4 · interpretation
The engine is best understood as a left fold over the additional arguments. The first argument is the initial accumulator; each newcomer is merged into that accumulator, and the result becomes the input to the next step. A plain-object newcomer produces an ordinary new object for that step, while any non-plain newcomer—such as an array, primitive, function, date, or class instance—is returned as the accumulator unchanged by the engine. Consequently, “non-plain values replace” applies even at the root, and a later plain object can in turn replace or merge over that value. With no additional arguments, `merge` returns the original first argument rather than making a copy.
Referent: clarification of the recursive merge engine, property copying, reference behavior, and callback-based variants
  Qualification: This clarifies rather than corrects the earlier account: its concise description is consistent with the inspected implementation, but “builds fresh objects” applies to plain-object merge steps, not to a call with no newcomers or a step whose newcomer is non-plain.

@investigram-e7adaf3e · interpretation
Recursion is driven primarily by the incoming value: it occurs when the prior value is not `undefined` and the incoming value is a plain object. If both values are plain objects, their properties combine deeply. If the prior value is defined but non-plain, recursion starts from an empty object and reconstructs the incoming plain object. If the prior value is missing or explicitly `undefined`, recursion is skipped and the incoming value is assigned directly. This explains the reference behavior precisely: origin-only properties are copied by reference; an incoming plain object with no defined counterpart is also retained by reference; only an overlapping, defined path whose incoming side is plain is rebuilt. Arrays and special objects are assigned as values rather than traversed.
Referent: recursive-merge trigger and nested reference retention
  Qualification: The implementation does not distinguish a missing prior key from an own prior key whose value is `undefined` when deciding whether to recurse.
  Qualification: The README similarly warns that nested references can remain linked, but its prose is user-facing guidance; the more exact branch behavior here comes from source inspection.
  Qualification: No cycle detection is visible in the recursive implementation, so this evidence does not support safe handling of overlapping cyclic plain-object graphs.

@investigram-dde06853 · interpretation
For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.
Referent: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step
  Qualification: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
  Qualification: Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
  Qualification: Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: Preserve only source enumerability while materializing each copied value as a writable, configurable data property.

referent.description: property creation policy applied by `assignProp`

qualifications: Enumerable properties use ordinary computed assignment; non-enumerable properties use `Object.defineProperty` with `enumerable: false`, `writable: true`, and `configurable: true`.

accounts.prose: Skip the literal string key `__proto__` in both passes.

accounts.prose: Visit every own newcomer key, recursively merge an overlapping plain-object value when eligible, then assign the newcomer-side result.

referent.description: second-pass newcomer precedence and recursive value handling

qualifications: Recursion requires a defined origin-side value and a plain-object newcomer value; an optional compare function can transform the value immediately before assignment.
This aspect does not claim that all assigned nested values are cloned; unchanged values can retain references.

accounts.prose: From a plain-object origin, carry forward only keys that the newcomer does not own.

referent.description: first-pass copying of origin-only properties

qualifications: This pass runs only when the origin satisfies `isPlainObject`; string and symbol presence are checked against the newcomer's corresponding own-key lists.

accounts.prose: Collect own string names and own symbols, including non-enumerable properties but not inherited ones.

referent.description: own-key discovery for origin and newcomer passes

qualifications: `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` supplies string keys and `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` supplies symbol keys; neither operation traverses inherited properties.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: Accessors are evaluated, not copied. Every non-`__proto__` origin key is read before the implementation decides whether the newcomer already owns the same key. On an overlap, that first origin read is discarded and the origin property is read again while processing the newcomer; consequently an origin getter can run twice, while the newcomer getter is read once before recursion or comparison. Any side effects, changing return values, or exceptions from those reads become part of the merge operation.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: Accessors are evaluated, not copied. Every non-`__proto__` origin key is read before the implementation decides whether the newcomer already owns the same key. On an overlap, that first origin read is discarded and the origin property is read again while processing the newcomer; consequently an origin getter can run twice, while the newcomer getter is read once before recursion or comparison. Any side effects, changing return values, or exceptions from those reads become part of the merge operation.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: `concatArrays` is a narrow conflict policy: when both old and new values are arrays it returns their concatenation; otherwise it returns the new value unchanged. `mergeAndConcat` feeds this policy into the same recursive engine, so nested array conflicts concatenate while other conflicts retain normal replacement behavior.

referent.description: array-concatenation merge policy

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.
Concatenation is shallow and uses the origin array's `concat`; no element-level recursive merge is evident.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

qualifications: The guard is equality with the literal string `__proto__`; no broader dangerous-key policy is inferred.

accounts.prose: Visit every own newcomer key, recursively merge an overlapping plain-object value when eligible, then assign the newcomer-side result.

referent.description: second-pass newcomer precedence and recursive value handling

qualifications: Recursion requires a defined origin-side value and a plain-object newcomer value; an optional compare function can transform the value immediately before assignment.
This aspect does not claim that all assigned nested values are cloned; unchanged values can retain references.

accounts.prose: From a plain-object origin, carry forward only keys that the newcomer does not own.

referent.description: first-pass copying of origin-only properties

qualifications: This pass runs only when the origin satisfies `isPlainObject`; string and symbol presence are checked against the newcomer's corresponding own-key lists.

accounts.prose: Collect own string names and own symbols, including non-enumerable properties but not inherited ones.

referent.description: own-key discovery for origin and newcomer passes

qualifications: `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` supplies string keys and `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` supplies symbol keys; neither operation traverses inherited properties.

corrections.reason: The earlier account unconditionally said every copied value is materialized as a writable/configurable data property. That is exact for the explicit non-enumerable `defineProperty` branch, but too strong for the enumerable branch, which uses ordinary assignment and can be intercepted by an inherited setter. The replacement retains the earlier descriptor-loss finding while qualifying the enumerable case and adding the materially relevant eager-read behavior.
qualifications: The correction narrows an overstatement; under the usual unmodified `Object.prototype`, enumerable assignment to the fresh accumulator normally does create the described own data property.
The earlier symbol-key observation remains valid and is retained with clearer distinction between the TypeScript annotation and runtime key identity.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: `concatArrays` is a narrow conflict policy: when both old and new values are arrays it returns their concatenation; otherwise it returns the new value unchanged. `mergeAndConcat` feeds this policy into the same recursive engine, so nested array conflicts concatenate while other conflicts retain normal replacement behavior.

referent.description: array-concatenation merge policy

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.
Concatenation is shallow and uses the origin array's `concat`; no element-level recursive merge is evident.

accounts.prose: This is the package-facing barrel: it implements no merge logic, but exposes `merge`, `mergeAndCompare`, `mergeAndConcat`, `concatArrays`, and the `Merge` type from two delegated modules. The README presents the package as recursive plain-object merging with special instances retained as values. One documented edge is overstated: `merge(x)` is said to always return a new object, but the implementation’s empty reduction returns `x` itself.

README statements are attributed documentation, not established behavior. The no-additional-arguments discrepancy follows directly from the implementation and README text.
The entry module uses wildcard re-exports, so its apparent API follows the compiler-observed exports of the delegated modules.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: `concatArrays` is a narrow conflict policy: when both old and new values are arrays it returns their concatenation; otherwise it returns the new value unchanged. `mergeAndConcat` feeds this policy into the same recursive engine, so nested array conflicts concatenate while other conflicts retain normal replacement behavior.

referent.description: array-concatenation merge policy

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.
Concatenation is shallow and uses the origin array's `concat`; no element-level recursive merge is evident.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: `assignProp` is the final descriptor-normalization step of the recursive merge, not a descriptor clone. The merge enumerates all own string names and symbols, reads values through normal property access, and then asks `assignProp` to retain only the winning source property's enumerability. Non-enumerable results are explicitly created as writable/configurable data properties; enumerable results use ordinary assignment and therefore have ordinary `[[Set]]` semantics rather than an unconditional own-property definition.

accounts.prose: Symbols are operationally supported because both loops combine `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` with `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`, and computed access, assignment, `propertyIsEnumerable`, and `defineProperty` accept symbol keys. The helper's `key: string` annotation is therefore narrower than its actual calls: symbol keys are forced through `key as string`, which suppresses the mismatch without converting the runtime symbol.

qualifications: This is a source-level observation; no emitted JavaScript was acquired.

accounts.prose: Enumerability follows the object whose value is actually assigned at that merge level: origin-only properties consult the origin, while newcomer properties—including conflicts and values transformed by recursion or the compare callback—consult the newcomer. The callback can replace the value but cannot directly choose the resulting descriptor. At nested levels, the same rule is reapplied by a fresh recursive accumulator.

referent.description: enumerability precedence across origin, newcomer, recursion, and comparison

qualifications: The policy is per property at each recursive plain-object merge boundary; special/non-plain values are assigned as values rather than traversed.
The acquired compare-function tests check transformed values, not resulting descriptors.

accounts.prose: Accessors are evaluated, not copied. Every non-`__proto__` origin key is read before the implementation decides whether the newcomer already owns the same key. On an overlap, that first origin read is discarded and the origin property is read again while processing the newcomer; consequently an origin getter can run twice, while the newcomer getter is read once before recursion or comparison. Any side effects, changing return values, or exceptions from those reads become part of the merge operation.

referent.description: property-read timing and accessor side effects before `assignProp`

qualifications: Invocation counts follow the two captured reduction loops for an overlapping own key in ordinary, non-proxy objects.
Proxy traps, mutations performed during enumeration, and accessor-thrown failures were not executed or covered by the acquired tests.

accounts.prose: For a non-enumerable own property, `propertyIsEnumerable.call` selects `Object.defineProperty` with exactly `value`, `enumerable: false`, `writable: true`, and `configurable: true`. Thus accessor identity, getter/setter functions, source writability, and source configurability are discarded. For an enumerable property, `carry[key] = newVal` normally creates an enumerable, writable, configurable own data property on the fresh ordinary accumulator, but it is not equivalent to `defineProperty`: an inherited setter installed for that key could intercept the assignment instead.

referent.description: descriptor transformation performed by `assignProp`

qualifications: The inherited-setter caveat concerns ordinary ECMAScript assignment semantics and is not exercised by the captured tests.

`__proto__` string keys are filtered by both merge loops before reaching `assignProp`, avoiding the standard `Object.prototype.__proto__` setter; the source does not similarly harden every possible inherited accessor key.

corrections.reason: The earlier account unconditionally said every copied value is materialized as a writable/configurable data property. That is exact for the explicit non-enumerable `defineProperty` branch, but too strong for the enumerable branch, which uses ordinary assignment and can be intercepted by an inherited setter. The replacement retains the earlier descriptor-loss finding while qualifying the enumerable case and adding the materially relevant eager-read behavior.
qualifications: The correction narrows an overstatement; under the usual unmodified `Object.prototype`, enumerable assignment to the fresh accumulator normally does create the described own data property.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.
Concatenation is shallow and uses the origin array's `concat`; no element-level recursive merge is evident.

`assignProp` is the final descriptor-normalization step of the recursive merge, not a descriptor clone. The merge enumerates all own string names and symbols, reads values through normal property access, and then asks `assignProp` to retain only the winning source property's enumerability. Non-enumerable results are explicitly created as writable/configurable data properties; enumerable results use ordinary assignment and therefore have ordinary `[[Set]]` semantics rather than an unconditional own-property definition.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

qualifications: Array recognition is delegated to external `is-what`.

The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

qualifications: `isPlainObject` and `isSymbol` behavior is delegated to external `is-what`; only its declaration barrel, not its runtime implementation, was inspected.
Property descriptors are not preserved wholesale: assigned properties become ordinary writable/configurable data properties, with only enumerability distinguished.
The callback receives `undefined` for a missing prior value and is still invoked, which is broader than the README's description of a function triggered when a value is overwritten.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.

accounts.prose: The merge engine folds newcomers left-to-right. Only plain objects recurse; primitives, arrays, dates/classes, and other non-plain values replace the prior value. For plain objects it copies own string and symbol keys, includes non-enumerables, skips `__proto__`, preserves enumerable versus non-enumerable status, and builds fresh objects while retaining untouched nested references. `mergeAndCompare` applies a callback to every incoming own property after any recursive merge—not only actual overwrites, despite the README wording.

referent.description: runtime recursive merge engine and API variants

accounts.prose: For a plain-object newcomer, one merge step has two passes. First it copies each own string or symbol property found only on a plain-object origin into a new `{}`. Second it visits every own string or symbol property of the newcomer and assigns that property, possibly after recursively merging its value. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` means non-enumerable string properties are included, while `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` adds symbols. The string key `__proto__` is skipped in both passes. Inherited properties are never enumerated. The result has the normal `Object.prototype`; source prototypes and full descriptors are not copied.

referent.description: own-property collection and assignment behavior inside one recursive merge step

qualifications: Assignment preserves only whether a property is enumerable. All copied values become writable, configurable data properties; getters and setters are read through ordinary property access and are therefore not preserved as accessors.
Although `assignProp` is typed with a string key, symbol values are passed to it at runtime through casts and are handled by the computed-property and descriptor operations shown in source.
Only the literal string key `__proto__` receives this special skip; this account does not generalize that check to other property names.
